Taking on the challenge of desoldering individual LEDs from a flexible strip and rewiring them onto a custom-spaced board is a classic maker move, but it has some massive technical hurdles you'll want to plan for.

Here is a breakdown of why a standard off-the-shelf strip won't quite fit, the math behind full piano coverage, and the mechanical realities of "pulling them apart."

1. The Key Math: Why 60 LEDs Won't Fit

A standard full-sized piano has 88 keys (52 white keys and 36 black/sharp keys).

  • The Problem: A strip with only 60 LEDs physically lacks 28 lights to cover a full keyboard.
  • The Pitch/Spacing: On a standard keyboard, the width of an octave (7 white keys) is roughly 164–165 mm. This means each white key center is spaced about 23.5 mm apart. Standard "60 LEDs per meter" strips have a spacing of 16.6 mm between LEDs. They are actually too dense for white keys, not too far apart!

If you want a two-row system (Row 1 for all 88 keys, Row 2 strictly for the 36 sharps):

  • Row 1 (All keys): Needs 88 LEDs.
  • Row 2 (Sharps only): Needs 36 LEDs aligned perfectly over the black keys.
  • Total: You need at least 124 LEDs for this project.

2. The DIY Reality: "Pulling Apart" a Light Strip

Standard addressable light strips (like WS2812B or "NeoPixels") are made of flexible copper PCB. While you can cut them at the designated copper pads between every single LED, completely desoldering the tiny Surface Mount Device (SMD) LED chips from the tape to put them on a new backing is a recipe for a headache.

  • Heat Damage: SMD LEDs are highly sensitive to heat. Desoldering them and then soldering wires directly to their microscopic pins without a PCB backing frequently melts the internal plastic casings or destroys the tiny microcontrollers inside each chip.
  • The Wiring Nightmare: Each addressable LED requires 4 connections: 5V Power, Ground, Data In, and Data Out. If you isolate 124 LEDs, you will have to hand-solder nearly 500 tiny joints and run an incredibly messy web of loose wires.

3. A Better Maker Blueprint

Instead of destroying a pre-made strip and wiring individual chips by hand, here are two paths that will save your sanity and look incredibly clean.

Path A: The "Cut and Wire" Method (Using the Strip's PCB)

Instead of extracting the bare chip, cut the light strip at the designated cut lines so each LED keeps its tiny piece of flexible circuit board and copper pads.

  • Buy a high-density strip (like 144 LEDs per meter).
  • Cut it into individual 1-LED segments.
  • Use thin, insulated solid-core wire to bridge the power, ground, and data pads from one segment to the next, gluing the segments down at your exact calculated piano-key intervals. This gives you solid solder pads to work with instead of frying bare chips.

Path B: Dedicated Rigid PCB (The Cleanest Look)

Since you are looking for perfect alignment, you could design a long, narrow custom printed circuit board (PCB) divided into a few modular segments to span the keyboard.

  • You can layout the exact 23.5mm pitch for the white keys and the offset spacing for the sharps.
  • Buy bare WS2812B (or similar) LED chips in bulk.
  • Use solder paste and a hot plate or hot air station to easily reflow them onto your custom board.

Because you only need two colors to coordinate left and right hands, addressable LEDs are perfect. You won't need complex RGB color mixing. In your code (using an Arduino, Raspberry Pi Pico, or similar microcontroller), you can simply split your data array or listen to MIDI inputs:

  • Left-hand range: Light up designated indices as Color A (e.g., Blue).
  • Right-hand range: Light up designated indices as Color B (e.g., Green).

turns.prompt_text: Okay so I see there are three wires that connect to this LED strip. How many volts does this take?
turns.response_html:
This LED strip runs strictly on 5V DC.

Connecting it to 12V (or any higher voltage) will immediately fry the internal microcontrollers inside every single LED.

What the 3 Wires Do

Standard WS2812B strips use a 3-wire color code (usually terminated in a small plastic JST connector):

  • Red Wire (+5V / VCC): Connects to the +5V terminal of your power supply.
  • White or Black Wire (GND): Connects to Ground / 0V. (This must be tied to both the power supply ground and your microcontroller's ground so they share a common reference).
  • Green Wire (DATA / Din): Connects to one Digital GPIO pin on your microcontroller (Arduino, Pico, ESP32, etc.) to carry the serial lighting instructions.

Current & Power Requirements (Amperage)

While the voltage is fixed at 5V, the current depends on how many lights are on and how bright they are:

  • At 100% full-white brightness (all Red, Green, and Blue channels on), each LED draws about 50 to 60 mA.
  • For an 88-key piano setup (roughly 160–180 total LEDs across the strip):
    • Worst-case maximum (every LED full bright white): ~8–10 Amps.
    • Real-world piano practice (lighting up 6–10 keys at a time for a chord in single colors like Blue and Green): typically under 1.5 to 2 Amps.

A standard 5V / 4A (or 5A) DC power supply will give you more than enough headroom without running hot or dropping voltage across the keys.

turns.prompt_text: So to supply this power. Do I need a separate power converter? I have some esp32s and respirated pipe Pecos but I don't think those can supply the power to them
turns.response_html:
You are completely right: an ESP32 or Raspberry Pi Pico cannot safely supply the current this strip needs.

The onboard voltage regulators and GPIO pins on those boards are designed to handle tiny signals (around 12–40 mA per GPIO pin, and a maximum of a few hundred milliamps through the onboard 3.3V/5V rails). Trying to power over 100 high-density LEDs directly through the board's header pins will overheat the board's trace lines, brown out the microcontroller, or blow the onboard diode.

You do need an external 5V power source, but you have a few clean ways to wire it without cluttering your bench.

Option 1: Standard 5V "Wall Wart" (Easiest & Cleanest)

Grab a dedicated 5V DC / 4A (or 5A) power brick with a standard 5.5mm barrel plug.

  • Use a screw-terminal barrel jack adapter to split the power.
  • The +5V line goes directly to the LED strip's power leads.
  • Ground goes to both the LED strip and your microcontroller.

Option 2: Repurposing a 12V Supply with a Buck Converter

If you already have a standard 12V bench power supply lying around, you don't need a whole new AC power brick. You can simply wire in a cheap DC-DC Step-Down (Buck) Converter (like an LM2596 or XL4015 board).

  • Input: 12V from your existing supply.
  • Output: Dial the potentiometer down to a steady 5.0V (verify with a multimeter before connecting the strip).
  • A 5A buck converter costs around $3–$5 and lets you safely tap into any higher-voltage DC rail on your bench.

Option 3: USB-C 5V Phone Charger (Bench Hack)

If you have a modern 5V/3A USB-C phone charger or power bank:

  • Solder a bare 2-wire USB-A or USB-C breakout cable directly to your power bus.
  • Since you are only illuminating a few keys at a time for chord progressions (rather than blasting the entire 88-key strip in pure white), a solid 5V / 2.4A to 3A USB wall adapter easily provides enough current for practice sessions without dropping voltage.

The Wiring Schematic (Shared Ground)

No matter which 5V source you choose, wire the microcontroller in parallel, never in series:

[5V Power Supply (+)] ──────────────────────────────> Strip +5V
                                             │
                                             └──────> ESP32/Pico (5V / VBUS Pin)

[Power Supply Ground (-)] ──────────────────────────> Strip GND
                                             │
                                             └──────> ESP32/Pico (GND Pin)

[ESP32 / Pico (GPIO Pin)] ──[330Ω Resistor]─────────> Strip Data In (DIN)

Two Quick Hardware Safeguards:

  • Common Ground: The microcontroller and the LED strip must share the same Ground wire. If their grounds aren't tied together, the data signal won't have a stable voltage reference and your lights will flicker randomly.
  • Data Resistor: Placing a small 330Ω to 470Ω resistor on the data line between your GPIO pin and the strip's DIN pad absorbs voltage spikes and protects the first LED chip from frying when you power it on.

turns.prompt_text: So generally these hardware chips can output 3.3 volts Would that be enough to only activate the cords and not the entire LED strip?
turns.response_html:
No, 3.3V directly from the microcontroller is not enough to power the LED strip, even if you only light up a single chord.

Here is why:

1. The Power Issue (VCC Pin)

The WS2812B chips have built-in microcontrollers and internal RGB driver circuits designed strictly for 5V.

  • Even if an LED is turned "off" in your software (displaying black), its internal chip is still powered on, listening for data, and consuming roughly 1 mA of idle current.
  • If you connect the strip's main $5\text{V}$ power wire directly to a 3.3V pin on an ESP32 or Raspberry Pi Pico, the internal driver chips will be undervolted. The lights will either not turn on at all, glitch randomly, or freeze.
  • Furthermore, the onboard 3.3V regulator on those microcontrollers can only output about 300–500 mA total before overheating. Even lighting up just 6 to 10 keys (which is roughly 20 to 30 individual LEDs on a 144/m strip) can draw 400–600 mA, which exceeds what the board's regulator can safely deliver.

2. The Data Signal Issue (GPIO Pin)

Where 3.3V does come into play is the data signal from your GPIO pin.

According to the official WS2812B datasheet, when the strip is powered by 5V, it looks for a "logic HIGH" on the data line of at least $0.7 \times V_{CC}$, which equals 3.5V.

  • The 3.3V Logic Reality: Your ESP32 or Pico outputs a 3.3V data signal.
  • The Good News: In practice, about 90% of WS2812B strips will accept a 3.3V data signal directly without any issues, provided the data wire between the board and the first LED is short (under 6–12 inches).
  • The Fix if it Glitches: If you power the strip with 5V, send data from your 3.3V GPIO pin, and notice random flickering, you just need a cheap Logic Level Shifter (like a 74AHCT125 or a simple bidirectional level shifter board) to boost the GPIO data signal from 3.3V up to 5V.

The Cleanest Minimal Setup (No Separate Bench Supply)

If you want to power the whole setup from a single cable plugged into your computer or a standard 5V phone charger:

  1. Power the Microcontroller via USB: Plug a standard USB cable into your ESP32 or Pico.
  2. Tap the Board's Raw 5V Pin:
    • On an ESP32, use the VIN or 5V pin.
    • On a Raspberry Pi Pico, use the VBUS (Pin 40).
    • These specific pins bypass the 3.3V regulator and pull raw 5V straight from the USB cable.
  3. Run 5V to the Strip: Connect that VIN/VBUS pin directly to the LED strip's 5V line.

Since you are only lighting chords (6–10 keys at a time) rather than blasting the whole 88 keys in full white, a standard 2A USB port will easily supply enough current through the VBUS/VIN pin to power both the microcontroller and your active chord lights without needing a separate power brick.

turns.response_html:
This is neither a resistance nor an amperage problem—it is normal behavior for WS2812B addressable LEDs.

Addressable LEDs contain internal driver ICs that default to an off state ($0, 0, 0$) on power-up. Simply applying $5\text{V}$ and Ground will not illuminate them; they remain completely dark until a valid digital data signal is sent to the Data line (DIN).

Step-by-Step Verification

  1. Verify Strip Direction:

    • WS2812B strips are strictly unidirectional.
    • Look closely at the printed copper pads on the strip. There are small arrows pointing in the direction of data flow: DIN $\rightarrow$ DOUT.
    • The ESP32 data pin must connect to the DIN (Data In) end. Connecting to DOUT will result in no response.

  2. Establish Common Ground:

    • Connect the strip's Ground (white) to an ESP32 GND pin.
    • Connect the strip's Power (red) to the ESP32 VIN / 5V pin.

  3. Send a Test Data Signal:

    • Connect the strip's Data wire (green) to an ESP32 GPIO pin (e.g., GPIO 2 or GPIO 4).
    • Flash a minimal test sketch using FastLED, NeoPixel, or a MicroPython driver to drive the first few pixels.

#include <FastLED.h>

#define NUM_LEDS 10
#define DATA_PIN 4  // Connect to the green wire at DIN

CRGB leds[NUM_LEDS];

void setup() {
  FastLED.addLeds<WS2812B, DATA_PIN, GRB>(leds, NUM_LEDS);
  FastLED.setBrightness(50); // Keep brightness low for USB power testing
}

void loop() {
  // Light up the first 3 LEDs in blue for left hand test
  leds[0] = CRGB::Blue;
  leds[1] = CRGB::Blue;
  leds[2] = CRGB::Blue;
  FastLED.show();
  delay(1000);
}

Once the microcontroller transmits the first data packet over the GPIO line, the LEDs will immediately latch and display the programmed colors.

turns.response_html:
The Raspberry Pi Pico is an ideal board for driving WS2812B strips because its PIO (Programmable I/O) state machines handle the strict microsecond timing in hardware, freeing the main CPU completely.

1. Breadboard Wiring with the Pico

  • Power (Red wire): Connect to Pin 40 (VBUS). This routes raw 5V straight from your computer's USB cable directly to the strip.
  • Ground (White wire): Connect to any GND pin on the Pico (e.g., Pin 38 or Pin 3).
  • Data (Green wire): Connect to Pin 21 (GP16) or any preferred GPIO pin. Make sure you connect to the DIN side of the strip.

2. Minimal MicroPython Test Script

Flash this directly onto the Pico using Thonny. It configures a PIO state machine to transmit the standard WS2812B 800 kHz protocol over GP16:

import array
import time
from machine import Pin
import rp2

# Configuration
NUM_LEDS = 10       # Number of LEDs to test
PIN_NUM = 16        # GP16 (Physical Pin 21)
BRIGHTNESS = 0.2    # 0.0 to 1.0 (keep low for bench USB testing)

# PIO assembly program for WS2812B timing
@rp2.asm_pio(sideset_init=rp2.PIO.OUT_LOW, out_shiftdir=rp2.PIO.SHIFT_LEFT, autopull=True, pull_thresh=24)
def ws2812():
    T1 = 2
    T2 = 5
    T3 = 3
    wrap_target()
    label("bitloop")
    out(x, 1)               .side(0) [T3 - 1]
    jmp(not_x, "do_zero")   .side(1) [T1 - 1]
    jmp("bitloop")          .side(1) [T2 - 1]
    label("do_zero")
    nop()                   .side(0) [T2 - 1]
    wrap()

# Initialize State Machine 0 on GP16 at 8MHz
sm = rp2.StateMachine(0, ws2812, freq=8_000_000, sideset_base=Pin(PIN_NUM))
sm.active(1)

# Framebuffer: GRB format
pixels = array.array("I", [0 for _ in range(NUM_LEDS)])

def set_pixel(index, r, g, b):
    # Scale by brightness and pack as GRB
    r = int(r * BRIGHTNESS)
    g = int(g * BRIGHTNESS)
    b = int(b * BRIGHTNESS)
    pixels[index] = (g << 16) | (r << 8) | b

def show():
    sm.put(pixels, 8)

# --- Quick Test ---
# Light up first 3 LEDs in Blue (Left Hand)
for i in range(3):
    set_pixel(i, 0, 0, 255)

# Light up next 3 LEDs in Green (Right Hand)
for i in range(3, 6):
    set_pixel(i, 0, 255, 0)

show()
print("LEDs illuminated.")

Once this runs, the first 6 LEDs will immediately latch with low-power blue and green light. When you're ready, you can wire a couple of momentary tactile buttons to spare GPIOs (configured with Pin.PULL_UP) to step forward and backward through your chord index.
